newsitem.title: USA: Albright throws out ceremonial first pitch.
newsitem.headline: Albright throws out ceremonial first pitch.

text.p: Standing in for an injured President Clinton, Secretary of State Madeleine Albright took her profile-raising campaign to the Baltimore Orioles baseball stadium Wednesday and threw out the ceremonial first pitch of the season.

Dressed in a baseball jacket and cap bearing the orange and black insignia of the Orioles, Albright was greeted by cheers from a sell-out 48,000 crowd at Camden Yards stadium as she pitched to Baltimore catcher Chris Hoiles.

Clinton was originally due to make the pitch, a tradition that has been observed by presidents in many but not all years since William Howard Taft threw an opener for the defunct Washington Senators in 1909.
But after injuring his knee in a fall March 13, Clinton had to decline. The Orioles then asked Albright to stand in, and she immediately accepted.
The Orioles were originally supposed to open their season Tuesday against the Kansas City Royals but it was postponed a day due to high winds and plunging temperatures in Baltimore.

Undeterred by the delay, Albright rearranged her Wednesday schedule, bolted down a lunch with King Hussein of Jordan in Washington and raced in a motorcade 40 miles (65 km) to Baltimore to perform the time-honoured pitching ritual.
Although under the Constitution, the foreign-born Albright cannot fill in for Clinton as president, that did not stop her from replacing him on the pitcher's mound.
Aides said the 59-year-old Albright practiced her pitching Monday with her security agents at Andrews Air Force Base near Washington before boarding a flight to New York.
"She's been working at her slider. It's a wicked slider," said State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns.
Other aides said the secretary of state had been teased by one of her daughters, who said: "But Mom, you can't even throw like a girl."
Albright steadfastly refused to say in advance what kind of pitch she would deliver, saying merely: "However it comes out."
With no batter in position for the ceremonial pitch, and Hoiles standing well in front of the batter's box, Albright, a right-hander, managed a pitch that reached the catcher on the second bounce.
Apparently dissatisfied with her effort, she told reporters afterwards: "He (Hoiles) wanted a kind of curve ball. I'm not up for curve balls."
"I think I'll keep my day job," she added.

Albright's trip to Baltimore also had a political slant, coming as part of her campaign to raise her profile -- and by implication that of the State Department -- among an increasingly isolationist American public.
By contrast with her publicity-shy predecessor Warren Christopher, Albright has made meet-the-people trips within the United States a priority of her job since taking office in January.
